title: The IT Crowd: have you tried turning it off and on again?
description: The IT Crowd ran for four series on Channel 4 and gave every help desk its motto. Start with the characters, the running jokes and the awards. Then find out why turning it off and on again actually fixes things, and why not every "off" counts.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Roy answers the IT department phone. What does he ask callers, episode after episode?

options.text: "Have you tried turning it off and on again?"
"Have you tried clearing your cache?"
"What's your ticket number?"
"Have you read the manual?"

questions.explanation:
Roy first asks it in "Yesterday's Jam", the opening episode (2006), and keeps asking for the rest of the show. The joke lands because the advice is good. Real help desks start with a restart. It fixes a lot of problems for almost no effort, and it rules out the easy causes before anyone spends time on the hard ones.

The last two Questions explain why it works.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: The IT Crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_IT_Crowd), [Wikipedia: List of The IT Crowd episodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_IT_Crowd_episodes)

questions.title: In "Calamity Jen", a TV advert sings the new emergency services number. Type the number.
questions.description: Type it as one block of digits or in the groups from the jingle.
questions.explanation:
The number is **0118 999 881 999 119 725 3**: twenty digits, with a long pause before the final 3. Moss watches the advert and says it's easy to remember. Later in the same episode he sets the office on fire and reports it by email instead of calling anyone.

Real emergency numbers are three digits long for a reason. Someone in a panic, maybe in the dark or in smoke, has to dial one without thinking. The "0118" also points to a real change: in 2003 the UK replaced its directory enquiries number, 192, with a crowd of commercial 118 numbers.

questions.title: Which of these numbers reach the police, fire and ambulance services from a UK phone?
questions.explanation:
Both **999** and **112** reach the emergency services, and neither takes priority over the other. 112 is the emergency number across Europe. The UK added it in April 1995 on the same circuits as 999, so visitors who don't know the local number can still get through.

The other three are real numbers too, just for other things. 111 is the NHS line for urgent medical questions that aren't emergencies, 101 is the police non-emergency line, and 118 118 is one of the commercial directory enquiries services that the show's "0118" plays on.

questions.title: 999 is the oldest emergency telephone number in the world. In what year did it start in London?
questions.description: Enter a four-digit year. Answers within two years count.
questions.explanation:
999 started in the London area on **30 June 1937**. It was easy to dial in an emergency. Phones then had rotary dials, and 9 sits one hole away from the finger stop, so a caller in darkness or smoke could dial it by touch: put a finger in the second-to-last hole and turn the dial all the way, three times. Payphones of the time could also be cheaply modified to let the 9 through without a coin.

The IT Crowd's twenty-digit number would fail all of these tests.

questions.title: The IT department sits in the basement of which company?

options.text: Reynholm Industries
Wernham Hogg
Initech
Pied Piper

questions.explanation:
The show is set at Reynholm Industries, 123 Carenden Road in central London. Its founder and chief executive is Denholm Reynholm (Chris Morris). His son Douglas (Matt Berry) later takes over.

The other three are fictional companies from other workplace comedies: Wernham Hogg from the British *The Office*, Initech from the film *Office Space*, and Pied Piper from *Silicon Valley*.

questions.title: Jen Barber is hired to run the IT department. What does she know about computers?

options.text: Almost nothing: her CV claimed a lot of experience with computers, and her interviewer knew even less
She is a former systems administrator promoted into management
She built Reynholm Industries' first network
She is a programmer who refuses to answer the phone

questions.explanation:
Jen (Katherine Parkinson) says on her CV that she has "a lot of experience with computers". Denholm doesn't know enough to check, so she bluffs her way through the interview and becomes head of the department, which the show also calls relationship manager. In practice, her job is translating between the technicians and the rest of the building.

Real support teams often have someone like that: a person who explains problems to non-technical staff and manages expectations, even if they can't fix a printer themselves.

questions.title: Richmond Avenal (Noel Fielding) is kept in the server room. Why was he sent there?

options.text: He became a goth
He crashed the company's email system
He is the only person who can repair the servers
He was hired as a security guard for the servers

questions.explanation:
Richmond was once an up-and-coming executive at Reynholm Industries. When he became a goth, he was banished to the server room, out of sight of everyone else. It's a fitting spot for something a company would rather forget.

Real server rooms are built for machines. Fans push air through the racks and cooling keeps the hardware within a safe temperature range, so the rooms are loud and cold for anyone working inside.

questions.title: In 2007 NBC filmed an American pilot of the show. Which member of the British cast played the same role in it?

options.text: Richard Ayoade
Chris O'Dowd
Katherine Parkinson
Chris Morris

questions.explanation:
Richard Ayoade played Moss in both versions. The rest of the American cast was new: Joel McHale as Roy, Jessica St. Clair as Jen and Rocky Carroll as Denholm. NBC announced it as a series for the 2007 to 2008 season, but it never aired. The pilot leaked online in 2012.

In the British version, Chris O'Dowd played Roy, Katherine Parkinson played Jen and Chris Morris played Denholm.

questions.title: In the Series 3 episode "Friendface", Jen talks Roy and Moss into joining Friendface. What is it a parody of?

options.text: Social networking sites such as Facebook
Video-sharing sites such as YouTube
Search engines such as Google
Webmail services such as Hotmail

questions.explanation:
Friendface is a social network, and the name is a thin disguise for Facebook. The episode aired on 19 December 2008. Facebook had opened to everyone only two years earlier, and joining a social network still felt new and a little embarrassing.

The episode hasn't dated much. Social networks still grow by pulling people you know, or used to know, back into your life, whether you want them there or not.

questions.title: What did The IT Crowd win in 2008?

options.text: The International Emmy Award for comedy
The Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series
The Golden Globe for Best Television Series, Musical or Comedy
Nothing; it won its first award after the final episode in 2013

questions.explanation:
The show won the **International Emmy** for comedy in 2008. The International Emmys are separate awards for television made outside the United States, so a Channel 4 sitcom can win one. The Primetime Emmys are for American shows and don't cover it.

British awards came next. The show won the BAFTA for Best Situation Comedy in 2009, and in 2014 Katherine Parkinson and Richard Ayoade won the BAFTAs for best female and male comedy performance.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: The IT Crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_IT_Crowd), [Wikipedia: International Emmy Award for Best Comedy Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award_for_Best_Comedy_Series)

questions.title: Counting only the four regular series, how many episodes of The IT Crowd are there?
questions.explanation:
There are **24**: four series of six episodes each, from 2006 to 2010. Short series are normal for British sitcoms, which often have one or two writers. The IT Crowd had just one. An American network comedy of the same era usually ran for more than 20 episodes a season, written by a room of writers.

A 48-minute special, "The Internet Is Coming", aired on 27 September 2013 and ended the show, bringing the total to 25.

questions.title: Which of these lines are from The IT Crowd?

options.text: "Have you tried turning it off and on again?"
"Did you see that ludicrous display last night?"
"Dear Sir stroke Madam, I am writing to inform you of a fire…"
"Bazinga!"
"I'm not superstitious, but I am a little stitious."

questions.explanation:
Three are real. Roy's catchphrase runs through the whole series. "Did you see that ludicrous display last night?" comes from "Are We Not Men?" (Series 3). Roy and Moss memorise football small talk from a website so they can pass as fans, and the reply they learn is a complaint that Arsenal's Wenger brought Walcott on too early. In "Calamity Jen", Moss starts his fire email with "Dear Sir stroke Madam", decides that's too formal, and changes it to "Fire, exclamation mark".

The other two come from American sitcoms. "Bazinga!" is Sheldon's catchphrase in *The Big Bang Theory*, and the "stitious" line is Michael Scott's in the American *The Office*.

questions.title: Why does turning a computer off and on again fix so many problems?

options.text: It throws away state that has built up: leaked memory, stuck processes, stale connections and caches
It installs any pending software updates
It cools the processor enough to stop calculation errors
It resets the hardware clock, which drifts over time

questions.explanation:
A running computer keeps a lot of state in memory: open files, network connections, caches, locks and the internal flags of every program. Bugs damage that state a little at a time. A program with a **memory leak** forgets to give memory back, so it uses a bit more every hour. A process waiting for a lock that nobody releases waits forever. A network connection whose other end has gone away still looks open.

A restart throws all of that away. Every program starts again from its initial state, which has been tested far more than day 40 of uptime ever was. The chart shows the catch: the bug is still in the code, so the problems build up again. Engineers call this **software aging**. Some systems restart on a schedule to stay ahead of it, a practice called software rejuvenation.

Some restarts also install updates, but that isn't what unfreezes a program. A reboot doesn't cool the processor in any useful way, and it doesn't reset the real-time clock, which runs on a battery so it keeps time through a restart.

images.alt: Line chart of memory in use over days of uptime. From a clean start, the line climbs steadily as leaked memory piles up. At each reboot it drops straight back to the starting level, then climbs again at the same rate. A dashed line near the top marks running out of memory, labelled slowdowns, freezes and crashes. After the last reboot the line is climbing towards it again, labelled bug still there, climbing again.
images.caption: An illustration, not measured data. Chart: Quizbun.

questions.references: [Wikipedia: Software aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_aging), [Wikipedia: Memory leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_leak). For real systems that crashed after running too long, see the Quiz "Have you tried turning it off and on again? Real bugs a reboot hides".

questions.title: On a Windows 10 or 11 PC with default settings, which one starts the Windows kernel from scratch?

options.text: Restart
Shut down, then press the power button
Both give an equally fresh start
Neither; only unplugging the power cable does

questions.explanation:
Since Windows 8, **Fast Startup** has been on by default. When you choose Shut down, Windows closes your apps and signs you out, but it keeps the kernel session. It saves the kernel and loaded drivers to the hibernation file, `hiberfil.sys`, and loads them back the next time you power on. Startup is faster, but any bad state in the kernel or a driver comes back too.

Microsoft's documentation says Fast Startup doesn't apply to Restart. Restart runs the full boot, because people restart when they want Windows completely fresh. So when the help desk says "turn it off and on again" on a modern Windows PC, Restart is the button that does it.

If you shut your PC down every night and it still feels sluggish after a few weeks, try Restart instead.
questions.references: [Microsoft Learn: Fast startup causes hibernation or shutdown to fail](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-client/setup-upgrade-and-drivers/fast-startup-causes-system-hibernation-shutdown-fail), [Microsoft Learn: Distinguishing fast startup from wake-from-hibernation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/kernel/distinguishing-fast-startup-from-wake-from-hibernation)
